title: From Latin to Romance
intro:
Romance words are Latin words that never stopped being spoken. Their changes are regular — linguists call them sound laws — so a handful of rules lets you see *nocte(m)* inside *notte*, *noche*, *nuit*, *noite* and *noapte*.

Latin nouns and adjectives are quoted in the accusative singular, the form most Romance nouns descend from, with the final *-m* in brackets because it had stopped being pronounced long before. A dash (—) means the language has no inherited descendant; a word in brackets after the dash is the word used instead, and a word in brackets on its own is a learned borrowing.

items.title: Ten vowels become seven
items.sub: How Latin vowel length turned into vowel quality

rule.la: ī ĭ ē ĕ a ŏ ō ŭ ū
rule.it: i e ɛ a ɔ o u

items.p:
Classical Latin had five vowel qualities, each of them long or short, and length alone could tell words apart: *mălum* ‘evil’, *mālum* ‘apple’. In everyday speech length gave way to quality: long vowels were said with the tongue higher (close), short ones lower (open), and two pairs merged. Short *ĭ* fell together with long *ē* as a close [e]; short *ŭ* fell together with long *ō* as a close [o].

The result is the seven-vowel system behind Italian, Spanish, Portuguese and French: i, e, ɛ, a, ɔ, o, u. That is why a Latin short *i* or *u* so often turns up as *e* or *o*: *pilu(m)* → *pelo*, *bucca* → *bocca*, *boca*. Italian and Portuguese still distinguish all seven under stress; Spanish turned the open ɛ and ɔ into *ie* and *ue* (next two tables) and was left with five.

Romanian followed a slightly different, ‘Balkan’ pattern: *ĭ* and *ē* merged as in the West, but short *ŭ* stayed with *ū* as *u* — compare Spanish *lobo* with Romanian *lup*, and Romanian *bucă* below.
gloss: ŭ → o (ro. u): mouth (Latin ‘cheek’; ro. bucă ‘buttock’)

items.title: Foot, stone, hare
items.sub: Stressed short e breaks into ie
items.p:
A stressed Latin short *e* — by late Latin an open [ɛ] — tended to break into a diphthong. **Spanish** did it everywhere: *pie*, *piedra*, *tierra*, *siete*, *hierro*, *piel*. **Italian** and **French** did it only in an open syllable, one that ends in the vowel: *pe-de(m)* → *piede*, *pied*, but *ter-ra* → *terra*, *terre* and *sep-tem* → *sette*, *sept*. **Portuguese** never diphthongized at all; it keeps an open vowel: *pé*, *pedra*, *terra*.

Romanian has *ie* too (*miere*, *fier*, *piele*), but before an *a* in the next syllable it became *ia* (*piatră*), and after *ț* and *ș* the glide was swallowed: *țară*, *șapte*. Long *ē* never diphthongized anywhere: *tēla* is *tela* in Italian and Spanish. Italian *lepre* has no diphthong because Italian words stressed on the third-last syllable (Latin *LE-po-rem*) usually escaped it.

items.title: Good, new, fire
items.sub: Stressed short o becomes uo, ue, eu
items.p:
Short *o* — an open [ɔ] — went the same way as short *e*. Spanish has *ue* in every stressed position (*bueno*, *puerta*, *muerte*), Italian has *uo* only in open syllables (*buono*, *nuovo*, *fuoco*, but *porta*, *morte*), and French turned it into *eu* or *œu* (*neuf*, *feu*, *œuf*). Portuguese, once again, keeps a plain open *o*: *novo*, *fogo*, *porta*. Before a nasal French and Romanian have no diphthong: *bon*, *bun*.

Romanian *oa* is a different and later diphthong. It appears whenever the next syllable contains *a*, *ă* or *e* — *poartă*, *roată*, *moarte*, *doare* — and not otherwise: *foc*, *nou*. That is why Romanian alternates within one word: *frumos* but feminine *frumoasă*.

items.title: Gold, bull, thing
items.sub: The diphthong au
items.p:
Latin *au* (*aurum*, *causa*) was a true diphthong, like the vowel of English *how*. Italian, Spanish and French reduced it to a plain *o*: *oro*, *or*, *cosa*, *chose*. Spoken Latin was already doing this: Romans knew the rustic *cōda* for *cauda* ‘tail’ (hence Spanish *cola*, French *queue*), and the politician Clodius used the plebeian spelling of his family name, Claudius.

Portuguese stopped half-way, at *ou* (*ouro*, *touro*, *pouco*; in *coisa* it became *oi*), now pronounced simply [o] by most speakers; *pobre* is an exception with plain *o*. Romanian alone kept *au* intact: *aur*, *taur*, *auzi*. French *pauvre* only looks like another survivor: Old French wrote *povre*, and the *au* was put back later to match Latin *pauper* — it is still pronounced [o].
gloss: to rest → to put down (pt. pousar ‘to land, perch’)

items.title: Sea, nose, salt
items.sub: French turns stressed a into e
items.p:
In northern French a stressed Latin *a* in an open syllable (one that ends in the vowel: *ma-re*, *nā-su(m)*, *can-tā-re*) became *e*: *mer*, *nez*, *sel*, *père*, *chanter*. So every Latin verb in *-āre* ends in *-er* in French, and every past participle in *-ātu(m)* ends in *-é*: *cantātu(m)* → *chanté*, just as *prātu(m)* → *pré*.

In a closed syllable the *a* survived: *arbore(m)* → *arbre*, *parte(m)* → *part*, *carru(m)* → *char*. Before a nasal it became *ai*: *amat* → *aime*, *fame(m)* → *faim*, *mānu(m)* → *main*. The other languages kept their *a*, though Romanian darkened it to *â* before *n* and *m*: *cantāre* → *cânta*, *campu(m)* → *câmp*.
gloss: broad bean (es. haba, with f → h)

items.title: Eye, table, green
items.sub: The stress stays put; what follows it wears away
items.p:
The Latin stress almost never moved. Whatever happened to the rest of a word, its stressed syllable survived, and words wore down from the edges inward. Most exposed was the unstressed vowel just after the stress in words stressed on the third syllable from the end: *Ó-cu-lus*, *TA-bu-la*, *CA-li-dus*. Spoken Latin was already dropping it. The *Appendix Probi*, a late-antique list of ‘say this, not that’, warns ‘*oculus* non *oclus*’, ‘*calida* non *calda*’, ‘*viridis* non *virdis*’, ‘*masculus* non *masclus*’, ‘*tabula* non *tabla*’ — and the condemned forms are exactly what the Romance languages inherited.

French went furthest: it lost nearly every vowel after the stress, which is why French words are stressed on their last syllable. Italian and Romanian kept many three-syllable words whole (*tavola*, *lacrima*, *anima*, *lacrimă*); in Spanish and Portuguese such words are fewer, and often learned.

items.title: School, sword, star
items.sub: A vowel slips in before s + consonant
items.p:
Words beginning with *s* + consonant (*schola*, *spatha*, *stēlla*) were awkward for many speakers of late Latin, and inscriptions of the later Empire show spellings like *ispiritus* for *spiritus*: a vowel had slipped in front. Spanish, Portuguese and French all inherited it — *escuela*, *escola*, and Old French *escole*, *espee*, *estoile*. French later lost the *s* before a consonant and marks the spot with an accent: *école*, *épée*, *étoile* (the same lost *s* lies behind the circumflex of *fête* and *forêt*).

Italian and Romanian need no extra vowel: *scuola*, *spada*, *stella*, *școală*, *stea*. Older Italian did add an *i* after a final consonant, and it survives in set phrases like *per iscritto* ‘in writing’. English borrowed several of these words twice, before and after the change: *state* and *estate*, *squire* and *esquire*, *special* and *especial*.
gloss: shield (fr. écu also an old coin)

items.title: Hundred, sky, people
items.sub: c and g soften before e and i
items.p:
In Cicero’s Latin *c* was always [k] and *g* always [g]: *centum* sounded like ‘kentum’ and *Cicerō* like ‘Kikero’. In late Latin the tongue moved forward before the front vowels *e* and *i* (and the diphthong *ae*), and both consonants softened. The outcomes differ: *c* became [tʃ], as in English *church*, in Italian and Romanian (*cento*, *cer*); [θ], as in *thin*, in Castilian Spanish ([s] in Andalusia and the Americas); and [s] in French and Portuguese. *G* became [dʒ] in Italian and Romanian (*gente*, *ginte*), [ʒ] in French and Portuguese, and in Spanish it often vanished: *gelu* → *hielo*, *germānu(m)* → *hermano*.

Before *a*, *o*, *u* nothing happened — *casa* and *corpus* keep their [k] — except in French (see the next table). English shows the French value in every word it took from French: *city*, *cent*, *gentle*.
gloss: people (fr. gent and ro. ginte are literary)

items.title: Horse, field, goat
items.sub: French ca- becomes cha-
items.p:
Northern French went one step further than its neighbours: *c* was softened before *a* as well, first to [tʃ] and then to [ʃ], spelled *ch*: *cantāre* → *chanter*, *campu(m)* → *champ*, *caballu(m)* → *cheval*. The *a* after it then usually became *e* or *ie*: *capra* → *chèvre*, *cane(m)* → *chien*. *G* before *a* followed suit: *gamba* → *jambe*, *gaudia* → *joie*.

The dialect of Normandy and Picardy did not take part — and Norman French is what England borrowed after 1066. So English sometimes has the same Latin word twice: *catch* (Norman) and *chase* (central French) both come from spoken-Latin *captiāre*; *cattle* and *chattel* both from *capitāle* ‘property’.

items.title: Already, game, judge
items.sub: Latin consonant i
items.p:
Latin *i* before a vowel at the start of a word (*iam*, *iocus*, *iūdex*) was a consonant, [j], like English *y*; much later, printers began to write it *j*. In spoken Latin it hardened: Italian *gi* [dʒ] (*già*, *gioco*, *giudice*), French, Portuguese and Romanian *j* [ʒ] (*jeu*, *jogo*, *joc*). Spanish too had [ʒ] in the Middle Ages, but in the 16th–17th centuries it turned into the throaty [x] of *juego* and *joven*. In a few words Spanish kept the old [j], spelled *y*: *ya*, *yugo*; before an unstressed *e* it vanished: *Ianuāriu(m)* → *enero*.

English *j* [dʒ] is the Old French pronunciation, frozen at the moment of borrowing: *judge*, *joy*, *jewel*, *journey*. French itself has since softened it to [ʒ].

items.title: Night, eight, milk
items.sub: What happened to Latin -ct-
items.p:
Few changes are as easy to spot as this one. Italian simply assimilated the *c* to the *t*: *notte*, *otto*, *latte*. In the West the *c* weakened to a glide [j] that joined the vowel before it — the stage Portuguese and French still show (*noite*, *oito*; *nuit*, *huit*) — and Spanish went one step further, fusing glide and *t* into *ch*: *noche*, *ocho*, *leche*. Romanian turned the *c* into a lip consonant: *noapte*, *opt*, *lapte* (more on this in the next table).

After *u* the Spanish *ch* did not develop: *fructu(m)* → *fruto*, *luctu(m)* → *luto* ‘mourning’. And words borrowed later from written Latin skip the whole process: Spanish *lectura*, French *lecteur*, Romanian *lector* and English *lecture* sit beside the inherited *lecho* and *lit*.

items.title: Fight, thigh, wood
items.sub: Romanian pt, ps, mn
items.p:
Romanian has a habit no other Romance language shares: a *c* or *g* before another consonant became a lip consonant. *Ct* gave *pt* (*noapte*, *lapte*, *luptă*), *gn* gave *mn* (*lemn*, *semn*, *pumn*, *cumnat*), and *cs* (Latin *x*) gave *ps* in *coapsă* — though not in every word: *laxāre* gave *lăsa* ‘to let’. The change of *qu* to *p* (*apă*, *patru*, next table) belongs to the same tendency.

Where Romanian has *mn*, the West has a palatal nasal: Italian and French *gn*, Spanish *ñ*, Portuguese *nh* — *pugno*, *poing*, *puño*, *punho* beside Romanian *pumn*.

items.title: Water, four, tongue
items.sub: Romanian turns qu and gu into p and b
items.p:
Latin *qu* and *gu* were single sounds, [kʷ] and [gʷ]: a *k* or *g* said with rounded lips. Italian, Spanish and Portuguese kept the rounding (*acqua*, *agua*, *água*; *quattro*, *cuatro*, *quatro*); French lost it in speech while keeping the spelling, so *quatre* is said [katʁ]. *Aqua* had an especially long road to French *eau*, pronounced simply [o].

Romanian turned the rounded consonant into a full lip consonant: [kʷ] → *p*, [gʷ] → *b*. So *aqua* is *apă*, *equa* ‘mare’ is *iapă*, *quattuor* is *patru* and *lingua* is *limbă*. Short, constantly used words escaped and just lost the rounding: *quandō* → *când*, *quāle(m)* → *care*. Italian and French gave up *equa* for *cavalla* and *jument* (from *iūmentum* ‘beast of burden’).

items.title: Key, full, flower
items.sub: Italian turns l into i after a consonant
items.p:
After a consonant, Latin *l* turned into the glide *i* in Italian: *cl* → *chi* [kj], *gl* → *ghi*, *pl* → *pi*, *bl* → *bi*, *fl* → *fi*. That is why Italian words so often look like Latin with the *l* knocked out: *chiave*, *pieno*, *fiore*, *bianco*. It happened inside words too: *templu(m)* → *tempio*, *ecclēsia* → *chiesa*.

French kept all these clusters (*clé*, *plein*, *fleur*, *blanc*). Romanian kept *pl* and *fl* (*plin*, *floare*) but softened *cl* and *gl* to *chi*, *che* and *ghi*, *ghe*: *cheie*, *chiar*, *gheață*. Spanish and Portuguese found their own solution, shown in the next table — with many exceptions such as *claro*, *flor*, *blanco*.

items.title: Call, weep, rain
items.sub: Spanish ll and Portuguese ch
items.p:
Spanish and Portuguese went furthest with the same clusters. At the start of a word *cl-*, *pl-* and *fl-* fused into a single palatal sound: Spanish *ll* [ʎ] (now [ʝ] for most speakers), Portuguese *ch*, today [ʃ] but [tʃ] in the Middle Ages. *Llamar* and *chamar*, *llorar* and *chorar*, *lluvia* and *chuva* are the same words. After a consonant inside a word Spanish has *ch* as well: *amplu(m)* → *ancho*, *masculu(m)* → *macho*, *inflāre* → *hinchar*.

The rule has many gaps: words that came in later, or stayed close to the written language, kept the cluster (Spanish *claro*, *plaza*, *flor*, *plomo*; Portuguese *claro*, *flor*). Portuguese also has a second outcome, *l* → *r*: *blancu(m)* → *branco*, *platea* → *praça*, *plagia* → *praia* ‘beach’, *obligāre* → *obrigar*, *ecclēsia* → *igreja*.
gloss: to weep (it. piangere and ro. plânge < plangere)

items.title: Do, son, iron
items.sub: Spanish f- becomes h-
items.p:
Spanish alone turned Latin initial *f* into *h*: *facere* → *hacer*, *fīliu(m)* → *hijo*, *ferru(m)* → *hierro*. Medieval Castilian went on writing *fazer* and *fijo* long after people had begun to say [h]; the spelling with *h* became standard in the 16th century, and the [h] itself has since fallen silent. The change is often credited to speakers of Basque, which had no *f*; Gascon, spoken just north of the Basque Country, did the same thing.

The *f* survived before *r* and before the diphthong *ue*: *frente*, *fruto*, *fuego*, *fuerte*, *fuente*. Learned and later words keep it too: *fama*, *fiel*. Sometimes both appear side by side: *hablar* ‘to speak’ (from *fābulārī*) and the learned *fábula* ‘fable’.

items.title: Wolf, goat, wheel
items.sub: p, t, c between vowels
items.p:
Between vowels, the voiceless stops *p*, *t*, *c* weakened in western Romance. Spanish and Portuguese voiced them to *b*, *d*, *g* (in Spanish today soft fricatives): *lobo*, *rueda*, *amiga*. French carried on until they were gone or nearly so: *p* became *v* (*capra* → *chèvre*, *sapere* → *savoir*), while *t* and *c* vanished altogether (*vīta* → *vie*, *amīca* → *amie*, *focu(m)* → *feu*).

Italian and Romanian — east of a line that crosses Italy from La Spezia to Rimini — mostly kept them: *lupo*, *ruota*, *amica*; *lup*, *capră*, *roată*. Italian has a minority of voiced forms, probably from northern dialects: *lacu(m)* → *lago*, *strāta* → *strada*, *acu(m)* → *ago* ‘needle’.
gloss: to taste, be wise → to know

items.title: Pain, colour, moon
items.sub: Portuguese drops l and n between vowels
items.p:
Between vowels Portuguese (together with Galician) lost *l* and *n* in the early Middle Ages: *dolōre(m)* → *door* → *dor*, *colōre(m)* → *cor*, *salīre* → *sair*, *lūna(m)* → *lũa* → *lua*. A vanished *n* often left its nasality on the vowel before it — *mānu(m)* → *mão*, *bonu(m)* → *bom* — sometimes only for a while: *plēnu(m)* → *cheio*, *corōna(m)* → *coroa*, *vēna(m)* → *veia*. That is why Portuguese words are so often a syllable shorter than their Spanish twins: *dor* and *dolor*, *cor* and *color*, *céu* and *cielo*.

Romanian has its own rule for the same position: a single *l* between vowels became *r* — *durere*, *culoare*, *cer*, *sări*, and *ger* from *gelu*. Its *n* stayed: *lună*, *mână*, *vână*.
gloss: to jump (it. ‘go up’, es., pt. ‘go out’, fr. ‘jut out’)

items.title: Leaf, son, garlic
items.sub: l + i becomes gli, j, ill, lh
items.p:
When *l* stood before an *i* or *e* that was followed by another vowel (*folia*, *fīliu(m)*, *muliere(m)*, said [ˈfolja], [ˈfiːljum]), the two fused into the palatal [ʎ] — the sound of Italian *gli*. Italian writes it *gli*, Portuguese *lh* (a spelling taken from medieval Occitan, like *nh*), French *il* or *ill*, which is now pronounced [j]: *feuille* [fœj]. Spanish moved on from [ʎ] to [ʒ] and finally to the [x] of *hoja*, *hijo*, *mujer*, *ajo*.

The cluster *cl* produced when a vowel dropped out (*auricula* → *oricla*, *oculu(m)* → *oclu*) joined the same sound in the West: *oreja*, *oreille*, *orelha*. Italian has *cchi* there instead (*orecchio*), Romanian *che* (*ureche*). Romanian simply lost the [ʎ], leaving only the *i*: *foaie*, *fiu*, *ai*, *pai*. French *fils* is a special case: it continues the nominative *fīlius*, and its *l* is no longer pronounced.
gloss: woman (it. moglie ‘wife’; ro. muiere is rustic)

items.title: Vineyard, bath, lord
items.sub: n + i becomes gn, ñ, nh
items.p:
*N* before the same glide became the palatal nasal [ɲ], the sound of Italian and French *gn*, Spanish *ñ* and Portuguese *nh*: *vīnea* → *vigna*, *viña*, *vigne*, *vinha*. The Spanish letter *ñ* began as a scribe’s shorthand for a double *nn* (one *n* written small above the other), because Latin *nn* gave the same sound: *annu(m)* → *año*. Latin *gn* often joined in too: *pugnu(m)* → *puño*, *punho*.

At the end of a French word the palatal did not survive: *balneu(m)* → *bain*. Romanian, as with *l*, kept only the *i*: *vie* ‘vineyard’, *baie* ‘bath’.

items.title: Wine, drink, war
items.sub: Latin v and b, and Germanic w
items.p:
Classical Latin *v* was [w]: *vīnum* sounded like ‘weenum’ — which is why the Germanic peoples, who borrowed it early, still say *wine* and *Wein*. By imperial times it had become a fricative, and between vowels it merged with *b*; inscriptions confuse the two (*bixit* for *vīxit* ‘lived’). Italian, French, Portuguese and Romanian ended up with [v], and turned many a *b* between vowels into *v* as well: *habēre* → *avere*, *avoir*, *haver*; *caballu(m)* → *cavallo*, *cheval*, *cavalo*. Romanian often lost it altogether: *cal*, *bea*. Spanish never separated the two again: *vino* and *beber* begin with the same [b], and the letters *b* and *v* follow Latin spelling, not speech.

When Frankish and Gothic words with *w* arrived, Latin no longer had a [w] at the start of a word, so speakers substituted [gw]: *werra* → *guerra*, *guerre*; *wardōn* → *guardare*, *garder*. French even gave some Latin words the new *gu-*: *vespa* → *guêpe*. English took both versions from French: Norman *war*, *ward*, *warden* beside central French *guard*, *guardian*.
gloss: to watch → to keep (it. guardare ‘to look at’)

items.title: We, three, wolves
items.sub: Final -s: kept in the West, lost in the East
items.p:
Final *-s* divides Romance in two. Spanish, Portuguese and French (with Catalan, Occitan and Sardinian) kept it, so their plurals continue the Latin accusative plural: *lupōs* → *lobos*, *loups*; *caprās* → *cabras*, *chèvres*; *noctēs* → *noches*, *nuits*. French still writes the *s* but stopped pronouncing it centuries ago, except before a vowel: *les amis* [lez‿ami].

Italian and Romanian lost it. In some short words it left an *i* behind: *nōs* → *noi*, *vōs* → *voi*, *magis* → *mai*, *cantās* → *canti*, *cânți*. Their noun plurals continue Latin nominative plurals in *-ī*: *lupī* → *lupi*. Whether Italian *capre* comes from *caprae* or from *caprās* is still debated.

items.title: Thing and cause
items.sub: Inherited and learned words from one Latin word
items.p:
Romance received Latin twice. Once by inheritance — words passed from mouth to mouth for fifteen centuries and went through every sound change — and again by borrowing from written Latin, the language of the Church, the law and the schools, from the Middle Ages to today, with hardly any change. Where both happened to one word, the result is a pair of **doublets**: the inherited one worn down and usually homely, the learned one close to Latin and often abstract. French *chose* ‘thing’ and *cause* are both Latin *causa*; *loyal* and *légal* are both *lēgālis*.

In each cell the inherited word comes first and the learned one second; — means there is no such word. *Pēnsāre* split early, into ‘weigh’ (worn down) and ‘think’, literally ‘weigh in the mind’, which kept its *n* under the influence of the written word. English, which borrowed from French in every period, has doublets of its own: *frail* and *fragile*, *loyal* and *legal*, *royal* and *regal*, *sure* and *secure*.
gloss: to listen / to listen with a stethoscope

title: Grammar after Latin
intro: Latin grammar was not lost so much as rebuilt. Cases gave way to prepositions and fixed word order; new articles grew out of demonstratives; new tenses grew out of phrases with *habēre* ‘to have’. Each table puts the Latin starting point — often a spoken-Latin phrase rather than a classical form — beside its result in the five languages.

items.title: The wolf, the goat
items.sub: The definite article from ille ‘that’
items.p:
Latin had no word for ‘the’: *lupus* meant ‘a wolf’ or ‘the wolf’ as the context required. In spoken Latin the demonstrative *ille* ‘that’ was used more and more often and gradually weakened into an article — just as English *the* grew out of an Old English demonstrative. Italian *il*, Spanish *el* and French *le* all come from *ille* (or its accusative *illum*), and *la* from *illa*. The plurals follow the case pattern of their nouns: Spanish *los*, *las* and French *les* from the accusatives *illōs*, *illās*; Italian *i* from *illī*. Portuguese lost the *l*, as it does between vowels: *lo*, *la* → *o*, *a*.

Romanian attached the article to the **end** of the noun: *lup-ul* ‘the wolf’, *om-ul* ‘the man’, *capr-a* ‘the goat’, *noapte-a* ‘the night’ — like its Balkan neighbours Bulgarian and Albanian. The suffixed article still carries case: *lupului* ‘of / to the wolf’, from *illui*, a spoken-Latin dative.

items.title: A wolf, a night
items.sub: The indefinite article from ūnus ‘one’
items.p:
‘A, an’ is simply the numeral ‘one’ worn down by constant use — exactly as English *an* comes from *one*. All five languages built it from *ūnus*, *ūna*; Romanian’s feminine *o* is *ūna* reduced to its vowel (the numeral is still *una*).

There was no plural of ‘one’, and each language filled the gap differently: Spanish *unos* and Portuguese *uns* make a plural of *ūnus*; French *des* and Italian *dei* are ‘of the’ (*de* + article) used for ‘some’; Romanian *niște* goes back to Latin *nescio quid* ‘I don’t know what’.

items.title: I will sing
items.sub: A new future from cantāre habeō
items.p:
The classical future *cantābō* ‘I shall sing’ did not survive. Once *b* and *v* had merged between vowels, *cantābit* ‘he will sing’ sounded like *cantāvit* ‘he sang’, and speakers preferred a phrase: *cantāre habeō* ‘I have to sing’. Through constant use the two words fused, and the endings of the Romance future are still the present tense of ‘have’: Italian *ho, hai, ha* → *-ò, -ai, -à*; Spanish *he, has, ha* → *-é, -ás, -á*; French *ai, as, a* → *-ai, -as, -a*.

The join still shows in Portuguese, where a pronoun can sit between the two parts: *cantá-lo-ei* ‘I will sing it’ (formal style; Old Spanish could do the same). Romanian chose another verb, *velle* ‘to want’, as English chose *will*: *voi cânta*. In everyday speech it prefers *o să cânt*.

items.title: I would sing
items.sub: The conditional: infinitive + past of habēre
items.p:
The conditional was a Romance invention, built like the future but with a past tense of ‘have’: ‘I had to sing’ came to mean ‘I would sing’. Spanish, French and Portuguese used the imperfect *habēbam*, which is why their conditional endings match their imperfect of ‘have’: French *(av)ais* → *chanterais*, Spanish *(hab)ía* → *cantaría*.

Italian used the perfect *habuī* instead: *canterebbe* ‘he would sing’ contains *ebbe* ‘he had’. Romanian again went its own way, with an auxiliary placed before the infinitive: *aș, ai, ar, am, ați, ar cânta* — its origin is disputed.

items.title: I have sung
items.sub: The compound perfect with habeō
items.p:
Latin could already say *epistulam scrīptam habeō* ‘I have a letter (that is) written’, with the participle agreeing like an adjective. In spoken Latin the phrase became a tense: ‘I have written the letter’. French and Italian still show the old agreement when the object comes first: *la lettre que j’ai écrite*, *l’ho vista* ‘I have seen her’. Verbs of motion and change take ‘be’ instead: *sono venuto*, *je suis venu*.

Spanish *haber* became a pure auxiliary, and ‘to have’ in the sense of owning passed to *tener*. Portuguese went further and uses *ter* as the auxiliary itself — but *tenho cantado* means ‘I have been singing (lately)’; the plain past is the simple *cantei*. In spoken French and northern Italian the compound tense has pushed out the old simple past (*je chantai*, *cantai*), and Romanian *am cântat* has done the same to literary *cântai*.

items.title: Wolves, eggs, times
items.sub: Plurals in -s and plurals in vowels
items.p:
With the cases gone, each noun kept one singular and one plural. The West built its plurals on the Latin accusative plural, with its *-s*: *lupōs* → *lobos*, *loups*; *noctēs* → *noches*, *nuits*. Italian and Romanian, which lost final *-s*, built theirs on the nominative plural: *lupī* → *lupi*. French writes the *s* but no longer says it: you hear the plural only on the article, *le loup* / *les loups*.

The Latin neuter plural in *-a* lived on in the East. Italian has a group of nouns that are masculine in the singular and take a feminine-looking plural in *-a*: *l’uovo* / *le uova*, *il braccio* / *le braccia*, *il dito* / *le dita*. Romanian turned this into a whole third gender, the ‘neuter’ — masculine in the singular, feminine in the plural — and spread the plural ending *-uri* of *tempora* to many nouns: *timp* / *timpuri*, *loc* / *locuri*. In Spanish and Portuguese the old neuters simply became masculine: *huevos*, *ovos*.
gloss: arms (fr. bras is also the singular)
times (fr. temps is also the singular)

items.title: Clearly, slowly
items.sub: Adverbs from mente ‘with a … mind’
items.p:
Classical Latin formed adverbs with endings: *clārē* ‘clearly’, *fortiter* ‘strongly’. Spoken Latin used a phrase instead — an adjective with *mente*, the ablative of *mēns* ‘mind’: *clārā mente* ‘with a clear mind’. The phrase lost its literal meaning and *mente* became a suffix. Because *mēns* is feminine, the adjective before it is feminine too: Italian *chiaramente*, not *chiaromente*; French *clairement*, *lentement*, built on the feminine *claire*, *lente*.

In Spanish and Portuguese the two parts are still felt as separate words: in a series only the last takes the suffix — *clara y lentamente*. Romanian never adopted the pattern; the plain adjective does the job: *vorbește clar* ‘he speaks clearly’.

items.title: More, better, the most
items.sub: Comparatives with plūs and with magis
items.p:
Latin compared adjectives with endings: *altus*, *altior*, *altissimus*. Only a few adjectives used *magis* ‘more’ instead (*magis idōneus* ‘more suitable’). Spoken Latin generalized the phrase, and the Romance world split over which word to use: the centre — Italy and France — chose *plūs* (*più alto*, *plus haut*), while the edges — Iberia and Romania — kept the older *magis* (*más alto*, *mais alto*, *mai înalt*). Older forms often survive at the edges of a language area while the centre innovates.

The commonest irregular comparatives survived as single words: *melior* → *migliore*, *mejor*, *meilleur*, *melhor*; *peior* → *peggiore*, *peor*, *pire*, *pior*; *minor* → *minore*, *menor*, *moindre*. Romanian kept none: *mai bun*, *mai rău*. The superlative is the comparative with the article: *il più alto*, *el más alto*, *le plus haut*, *cel mai înalt*; *-issimus* lives on in Italian *altissimo* ‘very high’ and Spanish *altísimo*.

items.title: My, your, our
items.sub: Possessives from meus, tuus, suus
items.p:
The Latin possessives *meus*, *tuus*, *suus*, *noster*, *vester* (spoken Latin *voster*) survived everywhere. Spanish and French developed two sets: a full, stressed form (*mío*, *le mien*) and a short one used before the noun (*mi libro*, *mon livre*). Italian and Portuguese use the full form together with the article: *il mio libro*, *o meu livro*. Romanian puts the possessive after the noun, which carries the article: *cartea mea* ‘the book my’.

*Suus* referred back to the subject, so a new word was needed for ‘their’: Italian *loro*, French *leur* and Romanian *lor* all come from *illōrum* ‘of those’. Spanish and Portuguese use *su*, *seu* for ‘their’ as well as ‘his, her’.

items.title: To be
items.sub: sum, es, est and its heirs
items.p:
The most irregular verb stayed the most irregular in every language. Spoken Latin made its infinitive look like a normal verb, *essere* for *esse*: Italian *essere*, French *être* (Old French *estre*). Spanish and Portuguese *ser* also absorbed *sedēre* ‘to sit’ (Old Spanish *seer*), and both languages split ‘to be’ in two: *ser* for what something is, *estar* — from *stāre* ‘to stand’ — for where or how it is. Romanian *a fi* comes from *fierī* ‘to become’.

Some forms have surprising sources. Spanish *eres* ‘you are’ continues the Latin future *eris* ‘you will be’. French borrowed from *stāre* too: the past participle *été* comes from *stātum*, and the imperfect *était* from *stābat*. Italian uses *stare* for the progressive: *sto cantando* ‘I am singing’.

title: From Ancient to Modern Greek
intro: Greek has been written without a break for nearly three thousand years, and Modern Greek still uses the ancient spelling. Behind that familiar surface the sounds, the grammar and much of the everyday vocabulary have changed. Ancient forms are Attic, or Koine where Modern Greek continues the Koine form (*θάλασσα*, not Attic *θάλαττα*). Pronunciations are in IPA: [ð] as in *this*, [θ] as in *thin*, [ɣ] a soft voiced *g*, [x] as in *loch*, [ç] as in German *ich*, [ʝ] a strong *y*, [c] a *k* pronounced close to *ky*.

items.title: Six ways to spell [i]
items.sub: Itacism: η, ι, υ, ει, οι, υι all came to be pronounced [i]

rule.grc: η ι υ ει οι υι

items.p:
In Classical Attic these were six different sounds: ι [i], η a long open [ɛː], υ a rounded [y] like French *u*, ει a long close [eː], οι a diphthong [oi] and υι [yi]. Over many centuries they fell together, one after another, as [i]. The change is called **itacism**, after the medieval name of η, *ήτα*, pronounced *íta*.

ει had become [i] by the Hellenistic period and η by late antiquity; υ and οι first merged as [y] and joined the others only around the 10th century. The spelling never followed the sounds, so Modern Greek writes [i] in six ways: *ψυχή* is read *psichí*, *ειρήνη* *iríni*, *οίκος* *íkos*, *υιός* *iós*. For Greek schoolchildren this is the hardest part of spelling: the right letter can only be known from the word’s history.

Latin borrowed most Greek words before these mergers, which is why English still keeps the vowels apart: *psyche* (υ), *irenic* (ει), *economy* (οι), *helium* (η).

items.title: αι, αυ, ευ
items.sub: Diphthongs that became one vowel, or a vowel plus [v] or [f]
items.p:
Ancient Greek had a full set of diphthongs. Apart from those swallowed by itacism, two developments matter for reading Modern Greek.

**αι** became a simple [e], the same sound as ε: *παιδί* is [peˈði], *αίμα* [ˈema]. Latin had written it *ae*, which is why English has both *paediatric* and *pediatric*.

**αυ** and **ευ** ended in [u], which hardened into a consonant: [v] before vowels and voiced consonants (*αύριο* [ˈavrio], *Ευρώπη* [evˈropi]), [f] before the voiceless θ κ ξ π σ τ φ χ ψ (*αυτός* [afˈtos], *ευχαριστώ* [efxariˈsto]). **ου** was already a plain [u] in Classical times and stays so: *ουρανός* [uraˈnos].

Latin *au* and *eu* preserve the older value, and English inherited them: *Europe*, *nautical*, *eucharist*, *autonomy*.

items.title: When β stopped being b
items.sub: β δ γ and φ θ χ became fricatives

rule.grc: β δ γ · φ θ χ

items.p:
In Classical Attic β δ γ were [b d g], as in Latin and English, and φ θ χ were *aspirated* stops [pʰ tʰ kʰ]: a p, t, k followed by a puff of breath. Between the Hellenistic period and late antiquity all six became fricatives, sounds made by narrowing the airway rather than closing it: β [v], δ [ð], γ [ɣ] (before e and i [ʝ]); φ [f], θ [θ], χ [x] (before e and i [ç]).

Since then Greek has had no single letter for [b d g]. Modern Greek writes them with two: μπ, ντ, γκ — *μπάλα* ‘ball’, *ντομάτα* ‘tomato’, *γκρίζος* ‘grey’. After a nasal the old stop often survived, as in *δέντρο* [ˈðendro] from *δένδρον*.

Latin heard the older sounds: it wrote β as *b* (*barbarus*) and φ θ χ as *ph th ch*, not *f t c*. English spelling therefore reflects Greek as it sounded two thousand years ago, and Greek names reach English in two shapes: *Βασίλειος* is *Basil* in English but *Vasílios* in Modern Greek, *Δημήτριος* is *Demetrius* but *Dimítrios*.

items.title: δῶρον → δώρο
items.sub: Losing the final -ν
items.p:
Final ν was always a weak sound in Greek, and in Medieval Greek it disappeared from most words. The biggest casualty was the ending -ον of second-declension neuters, one of the commonest endings in the language: *δῶρον* → *δώρο*, *ξύλον* → *ξύλο*. The accusative singular lost it too: *τὸν λόγον* → *τον λόγο*, *τὴν ἡμέραν* → *την ημέρα*.

The ν survives where something protected it: in the article and pronouns (*τον*, *αυτόν*), in the genitive plural (*των δώρων*), and in learned words (*το παν* ‘the whole’). Even the feminine article keeps it only before a vowel or a stop sound (κ, π, τ, ξ, ψ…): *την πόλη*, but *τη χώρα*.

English words of Greek origin lost the same ending by another route: Latin turned -ον into -um (*θέατρον* → *theātrum*), and English then dropped it (*theatre*).

items.title: παιδίον → παιδί
items.sub: Diminutives in -ιον became ordinary nouns in -ι
items.p:
Koine loved diminutives in -ιον: *παιδίον* ‘little child’, *ψωμίον* ‘a morsel of bread’, *ὠτίον* ‘little ear’. In everyday speech they gradually lost their ‘little’ and pushed out the base words, which were short and irregular (*παῖς, παιδός*; *οὖς, ὠτός*). Then the ending wore down: -ιον → -ιν, a form already found in papyri of the Roman period, → -ι.

The result is one of the largest noun classes of Modern Greek, neuters in -ι with plural -ια: *παιδί, παιδιά*. Unstressed initial vowels often fell along the way: *ὀψάριον* → *ψάρι*, *ὀμμάτιον* → *μάτι*. *Αυτί* is pronounced *aftí*.

The old base words did not die; they live on in learned compounds such as *παιδαγωγός*, *Πελοπόννησος* ‘island of Pelops’ and *ωτορινολαρυγγολόγος* ‘ear, nose and throat doctor’. Latin went the same way on its road to Romance: *auris* gave way to *auricula* ‘little ear’ (Italian *orecchio*, French *oreille*), *avis* to Vulgar Latin *aucellus* ‘little bird’ (Italian *uccello*, French *oiseau*).

items.title: νύξ → νύχτα
items.sub: Third-declension nouns rebuilt on the accusative
items.p:
The ancient third declension was the irregular one: the nominative often hid the stem (*νύξ*, gen. *νυκτός*; *ἐλπίς*, gen. *ἐλπίδος*). The accusative singular, though, showed the stem plainly and ended in -α: *νύκτα*, *ἐλπίδα*. Medieval Greek took that accusative as the new base form. Feminines simply used it as the nominative, which made them look like first-declension *χώρα*: *η νύχτα, της νύχτας*. Masculines added -ς to match the masculines in -ας: *πατέρα* → *ο πατέρας, του πατέρα*.

The table gives the ancient nominative and accusative. Two sound changes also show: κτ → χτ (*νύκτα* → *νύχτα*, as *ὀκτώ* → *οχτώ*), and νδρ → ντρ (*ἄνδρα* → *άντρας*).

Latin nouns went through a strikingly similar process: most Romance nouns continue the Latin accusative, not the nominative — *noctem* → *notte, noche, nuit*; *patrem* → *padre*.

items.title: The dative disappears
items.sub: Its work went to σε, με and the genitive
items.p:
The dative was already in retreat in Koine and had left everyday speech by about the 10th century. Its work was shared out.

**Place**: *ἐν* + dative merged with *εἰς* + accusative, and *εἰς* won; it shrank to *σε*, which fuses with the article (*σε + το* → *στο*). **Company and means**: *σύν* and the instrumental dative gave way to *μετά*, shortened to *με*. **Indirect object**: *σε* + accusative for nouns (*στο παιδί*), and for unstressed pronouns the genitive: *σου λέω* ‘I tell you’, *του λέω* ‘I tell him’.

A few frozen datives survive in learned phrases: *δόξα τω Θεώ* ‘thank God’, *εν τω μεταξύ* ‘meanwhile’. Latin lost its dative in the same way in most of Romance, replaced by *ad* + noun (French *à l’enfant*, Spanish *al niño*) — except in Romanian, which still has a genitive-dative case (*copilului* ‘to the child’).
rows: I give the book to the child

items.title: λύω → λύνω
items.sub: Old verbs rebuilt with a present in -νω
items.p:
Many ancient verbs had short or irregular present stems. Medieval Greek rebuilt them on the model of nasal presents such as *πίνω* ‘drink’ and *φθάνω* ‘arrive’, with a -ν- that belongs to the present only: *λύνω* ‘untie, solve’ but aorist *έλυσα*; *κλείνω* ‘close’ but *έκλεισα*.

The -μι verbs, the most irregular group in Ancient Greek, vanished as a class. Each was remodelled as an ordinary -ω verb, most of them in -νω: *δίδωμι* → *δίνω*, *ἵστημι* → *στήνω*, *ἀφίημι* → *αφήνω*, *δείκνυμι* → *δείχνω*. Their Modern aorists are *έδωσα*, *έστησα*, *άφησα*, *έδειξα*.

Other verbs simply wore down: *λέγω* → *λέω*, *τρώγω* → *τρώω*, *εὑρίσκω* → *βρίσκω*.

items.title: ἀγαπῶ, ποιῶ, δηλῶ
items.sub: Contract verbs became the conjugation stressed on the ending
items.p:
In Attic, verbs whose stem ended in α, ε or ο contracted that vowel with the ending: *ἀγαπάω* → *ἀγαπῶ*, *ποιέω* → *ποιῶ*, *δηλόω* → *δηλῶ*. The table gives both forms.

Modern Greek grammar calls their heirs **conjugation B**, verbs stressed on the ending. **B1** (*αγαπάω* or *αγαπώ, αγαπάς, αγαπάει*) continues the -άω type, and it attracted many everyday -έω verbs: *ζητάω, κρατάω, πατάω, φοράω*. **B2** (*θεωρώ, θεωρείς, θεωρεί*) continues the -έω type, today mostly in formal or learned verbs.

The -όω verbs left the class altogether and became ordinary verbs in -ώνω, like *λύνω*: *δηλόω* → *δηλώνω* ‘declare’, *πληρόω* ‘fill’ → *πληρώνω* ‘pay’.

items.title: No more infinitive
items.sub: να + a finite verb took over: θέλω γράφειν → θέλω να γράψω
items.p:
Ancient Greek used the infinitive constantly. Koine increasingly replaced it with *ἵνα* ‘so that’ + subjunctive, a construction already frequent in the New Testament, and by early Modern Greek the infinitive was gone. *Ἵνα* shrank to *να*, and every verb that once took an infinitive now takes *να* + a verb marked for person: *θέλω να γράψω* ‘I want that I write’, *θέλεις να γράψεις* ‘you want that you write’.

Traces remain. The perfect *έχω γράψει* ‘I have written’ contains a fossil of the old infinitive. Infinitives used as nouns became ordinary nouns: *τὸ φαγεῖν* ‘eating’ → *το φαΐ* ‘food’, and the learned *το είναι* ‘being’.

The loss of the infinitive is a **Balkan** feature, shared with Bulgarian and Albanian — and with Romanian, the one Romance language to do the same: *vreau să scriu* ‘I want to write’, literally ‘I want that I write’.

items.title: θέλω ἵνα → θα
items.sub: A new future from ‘I want that…’
items.p:
The ancient future (*γράψω*, *λύσω*, *ἔσομαι*) did not survive. Medieval Greek expressed the future with *θέλω* ‘I want’ followed by an infinitive or by *να*, and *θέλω να* wore down step by step: *θέλει να γράψει* → *θε να γράψει* → *θα να γράψει* → *θα γράψει*. Today *θα* is an invariable particle: *θα γράψω* ‘I will write (once)’, *θα γράφω* ‘I will be writing’. With a past tense it forms the conditional: *θα έγραφα* ‘I would write’.

The Latin future died too. Western Romance built a new one from *amāre habeō* ‘I have to love’ → *amerò, amaré, aimerai, amarei*; Romanian used *volō* ‘I want’, exactly as Greek did: *voi cânta* ‘I will sing’. English *will* also once meant ‘want’.

items.title: νερό, ψωμί, σπίτι
items.sub: Everyday words that replaced the classical ones
items.p:
Many of the most basic words of Ancient Greek were replaced in everyday speech. The newcomers were often diminutives (*ψωμί*, *ψάρι*, *μάτι*), descriptive adjectives (*νερό* is ‘the fresh (water)’, *άλογο* ‘the speechless (animal)’), words that once had a narrower meaning (*τρώγω* ‘munch’, *βλέπω* ‘look’, which replaced *ὁράω* ‘see’), or loans (*σπίτι* from Latin). The source of each modern word is given at the right.

The old words survive in the learned layer of the language, just as English has *eye* but *ophthalmologist*: *υδραυλικός* ‘plumber’, *ιππόδρομος* ‘racecourse’, *οφθαλμίατρος* ‘eye doctor’, *ιχθυοπωλείο* ‘fishmonger’s’, *ορειβασία* ‘mountaineering’, *ναυτικός* ‘sailor’, *οινοπνευματώδη* ‘alcoholic drinks’.

Latin went through the same renewal on its way to Romance: *equus* gave way to *caballus* ‘nag’ (*cavallo, caballo, cheval*), *domus* to *casa* ‘hut’.

items.title: σπίτι, παλάτι, κάστρο
items.sub: Latin words in Byzantine Greek
items.p:
The eastern Roman Empire spoke Greek, but for centuries its army, law and administration worked in Latin, and Greek absorbed hundreds of Latin words. Its people called themselves *Ῥωμαῖοι* ‘Romans’, a name that lives on in Modern Greek *Ρωμιός*.

The middle column gives the Byzantine form. Many loans were fitted with the Greek ending -ιον and then followed it to -ι (see *παιδίον* → *παιδί*): *hospitium* ‘guest lodging’ → *ὁσπίτιον* → *σπίτι* ‘house’, *palātium* → *παλάτιον* → *παλάτι*.

The same Latin words reached the Romance languages directly, so Greek *σπίτι* and Italian *ospizio* ‘hospice’, Greek *κάστρο* and Spanish *castro* ‘hill fort’, Greek *φούρνος* and Italian *forno* are distant cousins.

items.title: πόρτα, βάρκα, φουρτούνα
items.sub: Words from Venetian and Italian
items.p:
From the 13th century Venice ruled Crete (until 1669), the Ionian Islands (until 1797) and many Aegean ports, and Italian was the common language of Mediterranean ships and harbours. Greek took hundreds of words from Venetian and Italian, above all for the sea, the house and the kitchen.

Italian *b* is written *μπ* (*bagno* → *μπάνιο*), because Greek β had long since become [v]; Italian *gn* [ɲ] becomes *νι*. *Καπετάνιος* comes from the Venetian form *capitanio*. *Φουρτούνα* is the sailors’ sense of *fortuna*: chance, and then a storm at sea.

Some of these words were Latin before they were Italian, and *πόρτα* and *βάρκα* may already have entered Greek in Byzantine times.

items.title: καφές, τσάι, χαλί
items.sub: Words from Ottoman Turkish
items.p:
Four centuries of Ottoman rule — from the fall of Constantinople in 1453 to independence in the 1830s, and until 1912 in the north — brought thousands of Turkish words into everyday Greek. The Turkish source is given at the right. Many were Arabic or Persian before they were Turkish: *καφές* ← *kahve* ← Arabic *qahwa*; *κέφι* ← *keyif* ← Arabic *kayf*; *παπούτσι* ← *pabuç* ← Persian.

They were fitted into Greek declension: masculines in stressed -ές, -άς with plurals in -έδες, -άδες (*ο καφές, οι καφέδες*), neuters in -ι (*χαλί, χαλιά*). Turkish *ç* [tʃ] and *c* [dʒ] are written τσ and τζ.

After independence the learned language tried to drive them out, and many survive only in colloquial speech; those for food, drink and the home were too useful to replace.

items.title: εντάξει, κατά, ως
items.sub: Ancient words and phrases brought back by the learned language
items.p:
After independence the Greek state adopted **katharevousa** (*καθαρεύουσα* ‘the purifying one’), an archaizing written standard that revived ancient forms and coined new words from ancient roots. It remained the official language until 1976, when the spoken language, Demotic (*δημοτική*), replaced it.

Standard Modern Greek is Demotic, but it kept much of katharevousa: whole ancient phrases with the dead dative (*εν τω μεταξύ*), prepositions such as *κατά*, *ως*, *ανά*, *άνευ*, and thousands of words. *Εντάξει*, the Greek ‘OK’, is ancient *ἐν τάξει* ‘in (good) order’, written as one word.

Revived words often took on modern meanings: *ἐφημερίς* ‘daily record’ became *εφημερίδα* ‘newspaper’ (rebuilt on the accusative, like *ελπίδα*), *ξενοδοχεῖον* ‘inn’ became *ξενοδοχείο* ‘hotel’, and Byzantine *νοσοκομεῖον* became *νοσοκομείο* ‘hospital’.

items.title: One accent instead of five marks
items.sub: The monotonic reform of 1982
items.p:
The polytonic marks were devised by scholars in Hellenistic Alexandria (tradition credits Aristophanes of Byzantium, around 200 BC) to guide readers through the pitch accent and the h-sound: the acute, grave and circumflex accents, the smooth and rough breathings, and later the iota subscript (*ᾳ, ῃ, ῳ*).

By late antiquity Greek had lost both the pitch accent, replaced by stress, and the [h]. The marks became pure spelling, learned by rote. In 1982 Greece officially adopted the **monotonic** system: one mark, the *τόνος*, on the stressed syllable of every word of two or more syllables; no breathings, no grave, no circumflex, no iota subscript. The diaeresis stays (*ρολόι* ‘clock’).

Words of one syllable are unaccented, except where the accent tells two words apart: *ή* ‘or’ but *η* ‘the’, *πού* ‘where?’ but *που* ‘that, which’, *πώς* ‘how?’ but *πως* ‘that’. The Church and some literary publishers still use the polytonic.

title: Greek in Latin, Romance and English
intro: Latin borrowed from Greek for more than a thousand years — early on by ear, later from books — and passed those words on to the Romance languages and English. These tables show how Latin spelled Greek, which everyday Romance words are Greek underneath, how Greek roots became the vocabulary of science, and how some of them came home to Modern Greek.

items.title: φ → ph, θ → th, χ → ch
items.sub: How Latin spelled Greek consonants
items.p:
Latin had no aspirated consonants, so for Greek φ θ χ — in Classical times [pʰ tʰ kʰ], a p, t, k with a puff of breath — it wrote the nearest Latin sound plus *h*: *ph, th, ch*. Initial ῥ, pronounced with breath, became *rh*. Greek κ was always written *c*, even before *e* and *i*, because Latin *c* was always [k]: *κέντρον* → *centrum*. The letters Y and Z were added to the end of the Latin alphabet in the 1st century BC purely for Greek words.

English and French kept the Latin spelling, so *philosophy*, *theatre* and *rhythm* still show Greek letters through a Latin filter, and the *c* of *centre* and *cycle* now has the soft sound that later Latin gave it. Italian, Spanish and Portuguese respell by sound: *filosofia*, *filosofía*; *teatro*; *coro*; *ritmo*.

γγ was pronounced [ŋg], hence *ἄγγελος* → *angelus*; ξ and ψ are simply *x* and *ps*.

items.title: υ → y, αι → ae, οι → oe
items.sub: How Latin spelled Greek vowels and endings
items.p:
Greek υ was [y], a sound Latin lacked, so Latin borrowed the letter itself: *y*. The diphthongs αι and οι were matched with the Latin diphthongs *ae* and *oe* (ῳ too became *oe*: *κωμῳδία* → *cōmoedia*); ει, by then a long [iː] or [eː], became *ī* or *ē*; ου, a long [uː], became *ū*. The rough breathing was written *h*: *ἱστορία* → *historia*.

Greek endings were made Latin: -ος → -us, -ον → -um, -η → -a (*μουσική* → *mūsica*). English then trimmed many of them (*typus* → *type*, *mūsica* → *music*) and simplified *ae* and *oe* to *e* (*economy*, *comedy*), though British spelling keeps a few: *encyclopaedia*, *oesophagus*.

items.title: Pietra, piazza, bottega
items.sub: Everyday Romance words that are Greek underneath
items.p:
Greek words entered spoken Latin through trade, cooks, doctors, craftsmen and slaves, and once inside they changed with the rest of the language. *Petra* and *platea* followed the regular sound laws into every Romance language, exactly like native Latin words.

Some replaced native words: *petra* largely displaced Latin *lapis* ‘stone’, and *colaphus* ‘a punch’ became the general word for a blow (*colpo, golpe, coup*). Others shifted meaning: *πλατεῖα (ὁδός)* ‘broad street’ became the town square; *ἀποθήκη* ‘storehouse’ became an Italian workshop, a Spanish wine cellar and a French shop. Romanian *spată* means ‘shoulder blade’, while the other languages kept the sword.

The gaps: Spanish and Portuguese say *mantequilla* and *manteiga* for butter, Romanian *unt* (from *unctum* ‘ointment’). For oil, everyday Spanish says *aceite*, from Arabic *az-zayt* (Portuguese *azeite* is olive oil); *óleo* is the learned word.

items.title: Chiesa, palabra, tío
items.sub: Greek words passed on by Christian and late Latin
items.p:
The first Christians of Rome spoke Greek, and Christian Latin was full of Greek words: *ecclēsia* ‘assembly’, *episcopus* ‘overseer’, *angelus* ‘messenger’, *baptizāre* ‘to dip’. They became ordinary words and changed shape with the language: *episcopus* → *vescovo, obispo, évêque, bispo* — and English *bishop*.

*Parabola* ‘comparison, parable’, the word for the sayings of Christ, came to mean simply ‘word’ in most of Romance, taking over from Latin *verbum*. Romanian, cut off early from the West, went its own way: its church is *biserică*, from *basilica* (elsewhere a learned word for a grand church), and its ‘word’ is *cuvânt*, from *conventus* ‘assembly’. Romanian *episcop* came later, through Church Slavonic.

Late Latin also took plain household words. *Thīus* ‘uncle’ gave *zio, tío, tio*, while French *oncle* (hence English *uncle*) and Romanian *unchi* continue Latin *avunculus*. *Cara* ‘face’, from Greek *κάρα* ‘head’, lives on in Spanish and Portuguese *cara* and in French *faire bonne chère*, once ‘to put on a good face’ — the source of English *cheer*. And *dracō* ‘dragon’ became the Romanian word for the devil, *drac*.

items.title: Bio-, geo-, -logy
items.sub: Greek roots in the vocabulary of science
items.p:
A handful of Greek roots supply a large share of the scientific and technical vocabulary of every European language. A few of these words are genuinely ancient (*δημοκρατία*, *γεωγραφία*); most were coined in Western Europe from the 17th century onwards — *biology* around 1800, *photography* around 1839 — and Modern Greek then adopted them, giving each part its Greek form: *τηλέφωνο*, *φωτογραφία*, *υδρογόνο*.

English takes the roots in Latin spelling (*ph*, *y*, *ch*: see the first two tables), so *psychology* and *ψυχολογία* look different but are letter for letter the same word. The suffixes differ too: English *-y*, *-ic*, *-ist* came through Latin and French, while Greek uses its own *-ία*, *-ικός*, *-ιστής*.

items.title: Anti-, hyper-, syn-
items.sub: Greek prefixes and their Latin twins
items.p:
Greek prefixes are as productive in English as Latin ones, and many pairs mean the same thing: *hyper-* and *super-*, *hypo-* and *sub-*, *syn-* and *con-*, *peri-* and *circum-*, *meta-* and *trans-*. Often the Latin word was a deliberate translation of the Greek: *hypothesis* ‘placing under’ = *suppositio*; *sympathy* ‘suffering with’ = *compassio*; *periphery* ‘carrying around’ = *circumferentia*; *metaphor* ‘carrying across’ = *translātiō*.

The ν of *σύν* changes to match what follows — *συμ-* before labials, *συλ-* before λ — and English, through Latin, keeps the change: *sympathy*, *syllable*. *Ἀ-* ‘not’ becomes *ἀν-* before a vowel: *ἄτομος* ‘uncuttable’, *ἀναρχία* ‘having no ruler’.

items.title: Quālitās from ποιότης
items.sub: Latin words built on Greek models
items.p:
When Romans began to write philosophy and grammar, Latin had no words for many Greek concepts, so they built new ones piece by piece on the Greek pattern — **calques**, or loan translations. Cicero explains that he coined *quālitās* to render *ποιότης* (*ποῖος* ‘of what kind’ = *quālis*); *essentia* was made for *οὐσία*; Latin grammarians translated the whole Greek grammatical vocabulary.

The method could misfire. Greek *αἰτιατικὴ πτῶσις* is the case of what is caused or affected, but *αἰτιάομαι* also means ‘accuse’, and the Latin translators took that sense: *accūsātīvus*. Through Latin these words became the abstract vocabulary of every Western language: *quality*, *quantity*, *essence*, *subject*, *case*.

items.title: Round trips
items.sub: Greek words that came home to Greek from the West
items.p:
Greek words that went west sometimes came home centuries later, changed beyond recognition. Greeks call them *αντιδάνεια*, ‘back-loans’. The route of each is given at the right.

Some came back by sea, through Italian. *Κόλαφος* ‘a punch’ became Latin *colaphus*, Italian *colpo* ‘blow’ and finally Modern Greek *κόλπο* ‘trick’ — while the unrelated ancient *κόλπος* ‘bosom, gulf’ lives on beside it. *Πιάτο* ‘plate’ is another: Italian *piatto*, from Vulgar Latin *plattus*, from Greek *πλατύς* ‘flat’.

Others came back through science. Western scholars built *atmosphaera*, *ēlectricus*, *téléphone* and *oxygène* from Greek parts, and Modern Greek took them back in Greek dress. *Καμάρα* ‘vault’ made the longest journey: Latin *camera*, the *camera obscura* ‘dark chamber’ of early opticians, and at last the *κάμερα* of every Greek phone.

title: One meaning, nine languages
intro: The same everyday meanings across all nine languages. Latin and Romance verbs are given in the infinitive (Romanian without *a*); Greek verbs, ancient and modern, in the first person singular, their dictionary form. Where a language uses a word from a different root, that word is still given, and the note says where it came from. Ancient Greek is Attic unless noted.

items.title: One to ten
items.sub: The most stable words of all
items.p:
Numbers rarely change, and all nine languages descend from the same Indo-European numerals: *trēs, τρεῖς, tre, three*; *decem, δέκα, dieci, ten*. The differences are regular sound changes.

Greek turned an initial *s* into the rough breathing, an *h*: *sex, septem* but *ἕξ, ἑπτά* (as in *sāl* ~ *ἅλς* ‘salt’). English shifted *p* to *f* and *d* to *t* — *πέντε* ~ *five*, *decem* ~ *ten* — the same shift as in *pater* ~ *father*. Romanian turned Latin *qu* and *ct* into *p* and *pt*: *quattuor* → *patru*, *octō* → *opt*.

Modern Greek counts with neuter forms (*ένα, τρία, τέσσερα*); the masculines are *ένας, τρεις, τέσσερις*. Attic *τέτταρες* is *τέσσαρες* in Koine, and *εφτά, οχτώ, εννιά* are common spoken forms beside *επτά, οκτώ, εννέα*.

items.title: Twenty to a thousand
items.sub: Tens, a hundred and a thousand
items.p:
Latin -*gintā* and Greek -*κοντα* both go back to an old Indo-European word for a group of ten, so *trīgintā* and *τριάκοντα* are built alike. Romance wore the Latin forms down (*trenta, treinta, trente, trinta*), just as Modern Greek wore *τριάκοντα* down to *τριάντα* and *τεσσαράκοντα* to *σαράντα*. English -*ty* is the Germanic word for ‘ten’. *Centum*, *ἑκατόν* and *hundred* are related too.

Romanian is the exception: it counts ‘three tens’, *treizeci*, a pattern shared with its Slavic neighbours though built from Latin words (*zece* < *decem*). Its *sută* ‘hundred’ is a Slavic loan, while *mie* comes from the Latin plural *mīlia*.

French counts in twenties from seventy: *soixante-dix* ‘sixty-ten’, *quatre-vingts* ‘four twenties’. Belgian and Swiss French say *septante* and *nonante*.

items.title: Days of the week
items.sub: Planets, the Church, and two languages that count
items.p:
Two systems meet here. The Romans took the planetary week from Hellenistic astrology: days of the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn and the Sun. Italian, Spanish, French and Romanian keep the gods from Monday to Friday (Italian -*dì* and French -*di* are *diēs*). The Church renamed the weekend: Saturday became the Sabbath, *sabbatum* — French *samedi* and Romanian *sâmbătă* reflect a nasalized form, as in Greek *σάμβατον* — and Sunday *diēs dominica* ‘the Lord’s day’. English swapped in Germanic gods (Tiw, Woden, Thor, Frigg); of the Roman gods only Saturn survived.

Greek and Portuguese number the days instead. Greek counts from Sunday: *Δευτέρα* ‘second’, *Τρίτη* ‘third’, *Τετάρτη* ‘fourth’, *Πέμπτη* ‘fifth’; Friday is *Παρασκευή* ‘preparation’ for the Sabbath, Sunday *Κυριακή* ‘the Lord’s (day)’. Classical Greek had no week at all: these are the names of Christian Koine. Portuguese adopted the Church Latin numbering, *fēria secunda* ‘second holiday’ and so on, promoted in the 6th century by Martin of Braga, who objected to days named after pagan gods: hence *segunda-feira* ‘Monday’.

items.title: Months
items.sub: One Roman calendar everywhere
items.p:
All nine languages use the Roman months. The Roman year once began in March, which is why *September* to *December* mean ‘seventh’ to ‘tenth’. *Quīntīlis* and *Sextīlis*, the old fifth and sixth months, were renamed for Julius Caesar and Augustus.

The Greek cities each had their own calendar — Athens began its year with *Ἑκατομβαιών* in midsummer — but the Roman months spread through the Greek East under the Empire; the Ancient Greek column gives them in their Greek form of Roman and Byzantine times. Modern Greek has formal names in -*ιος*, used in dates (*1 Ιανουαρίου*), and popular ones, mostly in -*ης* (*Γενάρης, Φλεβάρης, Μάρτης*).

The Romanian names are 19th-century borrowings from Latin and French. The old folk names were descriptive: *cuptor* ‘oven’ for July, *brumar* ‘hoarfrost month’ for November.

items.title: Family
items.sub: Old kinship words and their replacements
items.p:
The core kinship words are shared Indo-European: *pater, πατήρ, father*; *māter, μήτηρ, mother*; *frāter, brother*; *θυγάτηρ, daughter*. Greek gave up its cognate of *brother* — *φράτηρ* came to mean ‘member of a clan’ — and used *ἀδελφός*, ‘from the same womb’.

Romance renewed several. Spanish *hermano* and Portuguese *irmão* come from *germānus* ‘of the same parents’; Italian *fratello* and *sorella* are diminutives; Romanian *tată* and *mamă* are Latin nursery words (*tata* ‘daddy’, *mamma*). Latin *uxor* ‘wife’ died out, replaced by *mulier* ‘woman’ (*moglie, mujer, mulher*) or *fēmina* (*femme*); Romanian *soț, soție* come from *socius* ‘companion’.

Greek *θεῖος* ‘uncle’ passed through late Latin *thīus* into *zio, tío, tio*, while French *oncle* (hence English *uncle*) and Romanian *unchi* continue Latin *avunculus*. Words for *child* are new almost everywhere: Italian *bambino* and Spanish *niño* are nursery words, Portuguese *criança* first meant ‘upbringing’ (from *creāre* ‘to raise’), and Romanian *copil* is of uncertain, probably pre-Roman, origin.

items.title: The body
items.sub: Worn-out words renewed with diminutives
items.p:
Everyday use wears body words down, and Romance and Greek renewed them in the same way, with diminutives and expressive words. Latin *auris* gave way to *auricula* ‘little ear’ (*orecchio, oreja, oreille, orelha, ureche*), exactly as Greek *οὖς* gave way to *ὠτίον* (*αυτί*). Almost every Modern Greek body word is an old diminutive in -ι: *κεφάλι, μάτι, αυτί, δόντι, χέρι, πόδι*.

Italian *testa* and French *tête* are Latin *testa* ‘pot, shell’, once slang for the head; *bocca, boca, bouche* are *bucca* ‘cheek’. Romanian often goes its own way: *inimă* ‘heart’ is *anima* ‘soul’, *gură* ‘mouth’ is *gula* ‘throat’, *picior* ‘leg, foot’ is *petiolus* ‘little foot’.

Beneath the renewals the old cognates still show: *cor, καρδία, heart*; *dēns, ὀδούς, tooth*; *pēs, πούς, foot*.

items.title: Colours
items.sub: Germanic white, Greek leeks, and a coin
items.p:
Colour words change fast. In the West, Germanic neighbours supplied several: *blank-* ‘shining’ gave *bianco, blanco, blanc, branco*; *grīs* gave *grigio, gris* (and, through Venetian, Greek *γκρίζος*); *brūn-* gave French *brun*; Frankish *blāo* gave *bleu*. Romanian, far from the Franks, kept Latin *albus* as *alb* (and *niger* as *negru*, as Italian *nero*, Spanish *negro* and French *noir* also did), and made its blue, *albastru*, from *albus* too. Everyday Portuguese says *preto* for black.

Modern Greek replaced nearly every ancient colour word. *Λευκός* gave way to *άσπρος*, from Latin *asper* ‘rough’ via Byzantine *ἄσπρον*, a newly minted silver coin; *μέλας* to *μαύρος*, from *ἀμαυρός* ‘dim’; *ἐρυθρός* to *κόκκινος*, from *κόκκος*, the kermes ‘berry’ that gave red dye — just as Portuguese *vermelho* is *vermiculus* ‘little worm’, the same dye; *χλωρός* to *πράσινος* ‘leek-coloured’; *ξανθός* (now ‘blond’) to *κίτρινος* ‘citron-coloured’. *Καφέ* is ‘coffee’, *μπλε* is French *bleu*.

The old words live on in learned compounds: *λευκοκύτταρα* ‘white blood cells’, *Ερυθρά Θάλασσα* ‘Red Sea’, *χλωροφύλλη*. Neither Latin nor Ancient Greek had a basic word for grey or brown: *cānus* and *πολιός* are ‘grey (of hair)’, *fuscus* and *φαιός* ‘dark, dusky’.

items.title: Sun, sea and sky
items.sub: The natural world
items.p:
Sun, star and wind are old and stable: *sōl, ἥλιος, sun* are cognates, as are *stēlla, ἀστήρ, star*, and *ventus, wind*. French *soleil* comes from a diminutive, *sōliculus*.

The replacements are the interesting part. Latin *ignis* lost out to *focus* ‘hearth’ everywhere. For ‘mountain’ most of Romance prefers *montānea* ‘mountainous (land)’ to *mōns* (which survives as *monte, mont*, and as Romanian *munte*). For rivers, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian took *rīvus* ‘stream’, French *rīpāria* ‘bank’. Romanian *pământ* ‘earth’ is *pavīmentum* ‘paved floor’ — *terra* became *țară* ‘country’ — and *copac* ‘tree’ is of uncertain origin. Modern Greek renewed water (*νερό*), fire (*φωτιά*, from *φῶς* ‘light’), moon (*φεγγάρι*, from *φέγγος* ‘brightness’; *σελήνη* is the scientific word), mountain (*βουνό*) and river (*ποτάμι*, a diminutive).

English *mountain* and *river* are themselves Romance, borrowed from French in the Middle Ages; *sky* is Norse. Attic says *θάλαττα* for Koine and Modern *θάλασσα*.

items.title: Animals
items.sub: Old names, nicknames and baby words
items.p:
The old Indo-European animal names show through: *mūs, μῦς, mouse*; *lupus, λύκος, wolf*; *bōs, βοῦς* and *cow*; *ovis*, Homeric *ὄϊς* and English *ewe*. *Porcus* gave *porco, porc* — and English *pork*, by way of French.

Many were replaced by colloquial words. Latin *equus* yielded to *caballus* ‘nag’ (*cavallo, caballo, cheval, cavalo, cal*), just as Greek *ἵππος* yielded to *άλογο* ‘the dumb (beast)’. Late Latin *cattus* reached all the western languages and Greek (*γάτα*), while Romanian *pisică* comes from a call to cats. Spanish *perro* ‘dog’ is of unknown origin; Greek *σκύλος* was once a puppy (*σκύλαξ*). The mouse was renamed everywhere in Romance: Italian *topo* is *talpa* ‘mole’, French *souris* and Romanian *șoarece* are *sōrex* ‘shrew’; Greek *ποντικός* is the ‘Pontic’ mouse.

Italian *pecora* ‘sheep’ is Latin *pecora* ‘livestock’; Greek *πρόβατον* is livestock too, ‘that which walks forward’; *αγελάδα* ‘cow’ is ‘the one of the herd’ (*ἀγέλη*).

items.title: Food and drink
items.sub: Bread, wine, cheese and the rest
items.p:
Food words mix the very old and the newly made. *Mel* and *μέλι*, *sāl, ἅλς* and *salt* are inherited from Indo-European; *vīnum* and *οἶνος* go back to a shared ancient word for wine, and English *wine* is an early loan from Latin. Latin *lac* and Greek *γάλα* are related too, though irregularly.

Modern Greek remade almost the whole table: *ψωμί* ‘morsel’, *κρασί* ‘mixture’ (wine was drunk mixed with water), *ψάρι* from *ὀψάριον* ‘relish’, *αυγό* from *ᾠόν*, and diminutives in -ι: *αλάτι, λάδι, τυρί*. Romance renewals are fewer. Cheese is *formāticus* ‘shaped in a mould’ in Italian and French (*formaggio, fromage*), while Spanish and Portuguese keep *cāseus* (*queso, queijo*), as does English *cheese*, borrowed by the Germanic peoples from Latin. French *viande* was *vīvenda* ‘things to live on’ before it meant meat.

Spanish *aceite* and Portuguese *azeite* are Arabic *az-zayt*; Portuguese uses *óleo* for other oils. Romanian *brânză* is not Latin at all, and its origin is uncertain.

items.title: Ten basic verbs
items.sub: Be, have, go, come, see, say, give, make, know, want
items.p:
Latin and Romance verbs are given in the infinitive, Romanian without its *a*; Greek verbs in the first person singular, since Modern Greek has no infinitive.

The basic verbs preserve a great deal of Indo-European: *esse, εἰμί* and English *is*; *īre* and *εἶμι* ‘I (shall) go’; *dare* and *δίδωμι*; *venīre*, Greek *βαίνω* and *come*; *cognōscere, γιγνώσκω* and *know*. But they are also among the words most often renewed. In Spanish and Portuguese ‘have’ is *tenēre* ‘hold’ (*tener, ter*); Romanian ‘go’ is *mergere* ‘dive’, while Italian *andare* and French *aller* are of disputed origin; ‘know’ is *sapere* ‘taste, be wise’ in the West (*sapere, saber, savoir*) but *scīre* in Romanian *ști*; ‘want’ is *quaerere* ‘seek’ in Spanish and Portuguese *querer*.

Modern Greek renewed ‘go’ (*πηγαίνω*, from *ὑπάγω* ‘go away’), ‘see’ (*βλέπω* ‘look’), ‘make’ (*κάνω*, from *κάμνω* ‘toil’) and ‘know’ (*ξέρω*, from *ἐξευρίσκω* ‘find out’). English *want* is Old Norse; the older English word for wanting, *will*, is a cousin of *velle*.

title: Words that changed their meaning
intro: Words keep their shape better than their meaning. Each table sets a Latin word beside its descendants, and the last column tells the story: the Latin meaning, an arrow, and what the word means now, with the languages in brackets where they differ. Many of these shifts began in the colloquial Latin of soldiers, farmers and kitchens, where a joke or a metaphor — ‘pot’ for ‘head’ — slowly became the ordinary word.

items.title: Hut, hearth, house
items.sub: Words for the home
items.p:
Classical Latin had two words for a house: *domus* for a town house, *aedēs* for a dwelling or temple. Both vanished from everyday speech. What replaced them was humbler: *casa*, a hut or cottage, became the ordinary word for ‘house’ in Italian, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian. In French it survives only as the preposition *chez* ‘at the home of’, and the house itself is *maison*, from *mānsiō* ‘a stay, a stopping place’ — the inns along Roman roads where travellers spent the night.

The same downgrading happened to fire: *ignis* gave way to *focus*, the household hearth, and the hearth became the fire itself. And *domus* lingers in Italian only in its grandest sense: the *duomo* is the cathedral, the house of God. *Palātium*, the Palatine hill where the emperors lived, gave every language its palace.
gloss: hut, cottage → house (fr. chez ‘at the home of’)
a stay, stopover → house (fr), inn (es), dwelling (it, literary)

items.title: Pot, beak, ham
items.sub: Body words from slang
items.p:
Body parts attract slang, and Latin soldiers’ and farmers’ slang became the Romance norm. *Testa* was an earthenware pot or a shell; joking about a ‘pot’ for the head (as English says ‘nut’ or ‘noggin’) turned it into the head itself in Italian and French, while the old word *caput* drifted towards ‘chief’ and ‘end’ (Romanian *cap* still means head). *Bucca*, a puffed-out cheek, pushed out *ōs* ‘mouth’, which was too short and too easily confused with *os* ‘bone’.

Animal words were applied to people: *rostrum*, a beak or snout, is the Spanish and Portuguese face; *perna*, a ham, is their leg; *gamba*, the hock of a horse, is the Italian and French leg. A small spatula, *spatula*, became the shoulder blade and then the shoulder — or, in Spanish, the whole back.
gloss: pot, shell → head (it, fr), forehead (pt), skull (ro)
head → chief (it, fr), end, cape (es, pt); still ‘head’ in ro

items.title: Nag, fig, beast
items.sub: Animals and the kitchen
items.p:
The noble *equus* survived only in learned words (*equestrian*); the everyday horse was the *caballus*, the workhorse or nag. Liver became *ficātum* because the prized dish was *iecur ficātum*, the liver of a goose fattened on figs — the adjective outlived the noun. *Mandūcāre* ‘to chew, munch’, a comic word in Latin, became ‘to eat’ in Romanian *mânca* and French *manger* (Italian *mangiare* was taken over from Old French), while Spanish and Portuguese *comer* comes from *comedere* ‘to eat up’.

*Bēstia*, any beast, shrank to a grass snake in Italian (*biscia*), a doe in French (*biche*), and — via a masculine form *bēstius* — any bug or critter in Spanish and Portuguese (*bicho*). *Pullus*, the young of any animal, settled on the chicken; *pōmum*, any fruit, on the apple in French and on the fruit tree in Romanian.
gloss: beast → grass snake (it), bug, critter (es, pt), doe (fr)
young animal → chicken (it, es), hen (fr, from pulla), chick (ro)
fruit → apple (fr; it. pomo, literary), fruit tree (ro)
hearth-baked (bread) → flatbread (it), big loaf (es), sweet bread (pt), rustic cake (fr)

items.title: Prisoner, elder, lady
items.sub: Words for people
items.p:
*Captīvus* ‘prisoner’ shows how pity turns into contempt: in Christian Latin a *captīvus diabolī* was ‘a captive of the devil’, and Italian *cattivo* now means ‘bad, naughty’, while French *chétif* means ‘puny, sickly’. Spanish *cautivo* and Portuguese *cativo* kept the old sense. Titles were made from ordinary words: *senior* ‘older’ became ‘lord’ and then the everyday ‘Mr’ (*signore*, *señor*, *senhor*), and *domina*, the mistress of a house, became simply ‘woman’ in Italian *donna*.

Family words narrowed or shifted: *cognātus*, any blood relative, is everywhere the brother-in-law, and *nepōs* ‘grandson’ became ‘nephew’ (Italian *nipote* and Romanian *nepot* mean both). *Īnfāns*, literally ‘one who cannot speak’, gave the French child but the Spanish and Portuguese royal prince, *infante*. *Pāgānus*, a villager, became the heathen — traditionally explained by the countryside being the last to turn Christian.
gloss: mistress of the house → woman (it), owner (es), lady (fr, ro), Mrs (pt)
speechless one → child (fr), prince (es, pt), foot soldier, jack in cards (it)

items.title: Comparison, chat, weighing
items.sub: Speaking and thinking
items.p:
Latin *verbum* ‘word’ lived on mainly in learned use — in grammar, and in the Church’s ‘In the beginning was the Word’. For the everyday ‘word’ speakers turned to *parabola*, a Greek loan meaning ‘comparison’ and, in the Gospels, ‘parable’; Christian Latin used it, and the verb *parabolāre*, for ordinary speech. It gave *parola*, *palabra*, *parole*, *palavra*. Spanish *hablar* and Portuguese *falar* ‘to speak’ come from *fābulārī* ‘to chat, tell stories’.

Thinking was described as handling objects. *Pēnsāre* ‘to weigh’ became ‘to think’ (*pensare*, *pensar*, *penser*); *computāre* ‘to reckon’ gave both ‘to count’ and ‘to tell (a story)’, as English *recount* does. Some verbs moved from thought to feeling: *cōgitāre* ‘to think’ became Spanish and Portuguese *cuidar* ‘to take care of’, and *quaerere* ‘to seek’ became *querer* ‘to want, to love’ — while in Italian and Romanian it means ‘to ask’.
gloss: to reckon → to count; to tell (a story)
to think → to look after (es, pt), to ponder (ro)
to seek → to want, love (es, pt), to ask (it, ro)
to ask → to beg (es, pt), to pray (ro)

items.title: Fold, lift, place
items.sub: Verbs of moving and doing
items.p:
*Plicāre* ‘to fold’ is the most famous case: Spanish *llegar* and Portuguese *chegar* mean ‘to arrive’, Romanian *pleca* ‘to leave’. A common explanation is nautical — sailors folded their sails on reaching port — and the Romanian sense is often explained by folding up one’s tent to move on. Italian *piegare* and French *plier* still mean ‘to fold, to bend’. *Adrīpāre*, ‘to reach the bank’ (*rīpa*), is another sailors’ word: *arrivare*, *arriver*.

Other verbs simply became more general. *Mittere* ‘to send, let go’ now means ‘to put’ (*mettere*, *mettre*, *meter*); *levāre* ‘to lift’ means ‘to carry’ in Spanish and Portuguese and ‘to take’ in Romanian *lua*; *collocāre* ‘to place’ became ‘to put to bed’ (*coucher*, *culca*) but in Spanish ‘to hang up’ (*colgar*). *Tornāre*, to shape on a lathe, became the everyday ‘turn’ and ‘return’ — and in Romanian *turna* ‘to pour’.
gloss: to fold → to bend (it), to arrive (es, pt), to leave (ro)
to reach the shore → to arrive (es., pt. arribar ‘to put into port’)
to send, let go → to put (es., pt. ‘to put in’)
to lift → to remove (it), to carry, wear (es, pt), to raise (fr), to take (ro)
to place → to lay down (it), to hang (es), to put to bed (fr, ro)
to turn on a lathe → to return (it, es, pt), to turn (fr), to pour (ro)
to try to catch → to hunt (it. also ‘to throw out’)

items.title: Thick, stocky, whole
items.sub: Size, shape and quantity
items.p:
Classical Latin said *omnis* for ‘all, every’ and *tōtus* for ‘whole, entire’. *Omnis* disappeared, and *tōtus* took over both jobs: *tutto*, *todo*, *tout*, *tot*. Several everyday adjectives were colloquial words that ousted the classical ones: *bellus* ‘pretty, cute’ replaced *pulcher* ‘beautiful’ in Italian, Spanish, French and Portuguese, while Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian also used *formōsus* ‘shapely’ (*hermoso*, *formoso*, *frumos*). *Grossus* ‘thick, coarse’ became ‘big’ in Italian and French, and *bassus* ‘stocky, squat’ — known in Latin mainly as a nickname — became ‘low’.

*Minūtus* ‘made smaller’ is ‘tiny’ in all five languages and more besides: the Italian *minuto* is also a minute (a ‘small part’ of an hour), and French *menu*, a detailed list, is the menu. *Dīrēctus* ‘straight’ moved into morality and law: *diritto*, *derecho*, *droit*, *direito*, *drept* all mean ‘right’ and ‘law’.
gloss: made smaller → tiny (it. also ‘minute’, fr. also ‘menu’)

items.title: Thing, step, crumb
items.sub: How ‘nothing’ and ‘not’ were made
items.p:
Negatives wear out and need reinforcing. Latin speakers said ‘not a step’, ‘not a crumb’, ‘not a drop’, and in French the reinforcement became the negative itself: *ne… pas* (*passus* ‘step’), *ne… personne* ‘no one’ (*persōna*), *ne… rien* ‘nothing’ (*rem* ‘a thing’). Today *pas*, *personne* and *rien* carry the negation alone, while *pas* and *personne* still also mean ‘step’ and ‘person’. Italian did the same with *mica* ‘crumb’: *non è mica vero* ‘it isn’t true at all’.

Spanish and Portuguese *nada* ‘nothing’ is what was left of *rem nātam* ‘a thing born, anything at all’ — the *nāta* survived, the *rēs* went — while *rēs* itself lives on as Spanish *res*, Portuguese *rês*, a head of cattle. French *on* ‘one, people, we’ is *homō* ‘man’ in its nominative form, beside *homme* from the accusative *hominem*. And *magis* ‘more’ became French *mais* ‘but’ and Italian *mai* ‘ever, never’.
gloss: thing → nothing (fr), head of cattle (es, pt)
